hypotheses.title: lzCompose callable by anyone, no endpoint/executor check
hypotheses.description: `lzCompose` has no modifier or check that `msg.sender` is the LayerZero endpoint or that `_from`/`_executor` are trusted. Any external caller can invoke it with an arbitrary `_message` payload. The function then decodes the message, approves and deposits `_from` tokens held by the router, swaps them, and sends ASD to an attacker-chosen `_dstReceiver` (or refunds to an attacker-chosen `_cantoRefundAddress`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a valid 224-byte `OftComposeMessage` with `_dstReceiver = attacker`, `_cantoAsdAddress` = a real ASD vault, `_minAmountASD = 0`. 2) Attacker calls `lzCompose(_from = whitelistedUSDC, guid, message, executor, "")` directly. 3) Router approves and deposits `_from` tokens it holds (from prior legitimate in-flight messages) into ASDUSDC, swaps to NOTE, mints ASD, and transfers ASD to attacker. 4) Alternatively set `_dstLzEid == cantoLzEID` to force a direct `ASDOFT.transfer` to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of any USDC/ASD tokens sitting in the router (in-flight compose funds), and arbitrary minting of ASD to the attacker at the expense of the protocol's NOTE backing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyEndpoint`/`onlyExecutor` checks (e.g., require `msg.sender == endpoint` and `_executor == trustedExecutor`) and validate `_from` against the whitelist before processing.

hypotheses.title: _refundToken sends native value to attacker-controlled refund address
hypotheses.description: `_refundToken` transfers `_nativeAmount` (up to `msg.value`) to `_refundAddress`, which is taken directly from the attacker-supplied compose payload (`payload._cantoRefundAddress`). Combined with the unauthenticated `lzCompose`, an attacker can route the router's ETH balance to themselves by triggering any refund path (invalid length, non-whitelisted, swap fail, etc.).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `lzCompose` with `msg.value = X` and a payload whose `_cantoRefundAddress = attacker` and a `_from` that is not whitelisted (or a malformed composeMsg). 2) `_refundToken` executes `payable(attacker).transfer(msg.value)`. 3) Attacker also drains any pre-existing ETH held by the router if `_nativeAmount` is set to the router's balance.
hypotheses.impact: Direct loss of native ETH held by the router; griefing of legitimate compose flows by draining gas/fee funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only refund native value to the original `composeFrom`/trusted refund address, and only after authenticating the caller as the LayerZero endpoint.

hypotheses.title: _depositNoteToASDVault calls arbitrary address with mint selector
hypotheses.description: `_asdVault` comes from the attacker-controlled `payload._cantoAsdAddress` and is invoked via low-level `call` with `ASDOFT.mint.selector` after approving it to spend the router's NOTE. There is no check that `_asdVault` is a legitimate registered ASD vault. An attacker can point it at a malicious contract that pulls the approved NOTE via `transferFrom`, or at any contract exposing a `mint(uint256)` that mints to the attacker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract with `mint(uint256)` that calls `NOTE.transferFrom(router, attacker, amount)`. 2) Attacker calls `lzCompose` with `_cantoAsdAddress = malicious` and a valid whitelisted `_from`. 3) Router approves malicious contract for `amountNote` and calls `mint`, which steals the NOTE. 4) `_sendASD` then also transfers/attempts to send ASD from the malicious address.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of NOTE held/approved by the router; arbitrary external calls from the router context.
hypotheses.recommendation: Maintain an owner-managed whitelist of valid ASD vault addresses and require `_cantoAsdAddress` to be whitelisted before approving/calling.

hypotheses.title: _sendASD performs arbitrary call to attacker-chosen address with value
hypotheses.description: In the cross-chain branch, `_sendASD` does `payable(_payload._cantoAsdAddress).call{value: _payload._feeForSend}(...)` where `_cantoAsdAddress` is fully attacker-controlled. This lets an attacker direct the router to send ETH to any address and execute arbitrary calldata from the router.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `lzCompose` with `_cantoAsdAddress = attackerContract`, `_dstLzEid != cantoLzEID`, `_feeForSend = routerBalance`. 2) Router executes `call{value: _feeForSend}` to attacker contract, which can also reenter or drain remaining funds. 3) Even if the call "fails", `_refundToken` then sends `msg.value` to `_cantoRefundAddress`.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of router ETH balance and arbitrary call execution in the router's context.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `_cantoAsdAddress` against a whitelist of legitimate ASD OFT contracts before making the value-bearing call.

hypotheses.title: asdUSDC withdraw rounds down, allowing dust accumulation and value leak
hypotheses.description: When withdrawing a USDC version with fewer decimals than asdUSDC (e.g. 6-decimal USDC vs 18-decimal asdUSDC), `amountToWithdraw = _amount / (10 ** (this.decimals() - ERC20(_usdcVersion).decimals()))` truncates the remainder. The user's asdUSDC is fully burned, but they receive less USDC than the burned amount is worth. The truncated dust remains in `usdcBalances[_usdcVersion]` and is effectively stranded, benefiting no one and breaking the 1:1 backing invariant.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits 1 wei of USDC (6 decimals) → receives 1e12 asdUSDC. 2) Attacker calls withdraw with `_amount = 1e12 - 1` (one less than full). 3) `amountToWithdraw = (1e12-1)/1e12 = 0`. 4) Attacker burns ~1e12 asdUSDC and receives 0 USDC. 5) The 1 wei of USDC remains locked in `usdcBalances` forever, and the attacker's asdUSDC is gone. Repeated across many users, this creates permanent accounting drift between asdUSDC supply and USDC backing.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of user funds (burned asdUSDC with zero USDC returned) and drift between `usdcBalances` and actual redeemable supply. Any user withdrawing a non-multiple of the decimal scale factor loses the remainder.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_amount` to be a multiple of the decimal scale factor, or round the withdrawal amount up (favoring the user) while ensuring `usdcBalances` remains solvent, or track sub-unit balances per user.

hypotheses.title: _sendASD transfers tokens after emit and uses untrusted cantoAsdAddress
hypotheses.description: `_sendASD` calls `ASDOFT(_payload._cantoAsdAddress).transfer(...)` where `_cantoAsdAddress` originates from the user-supplied compose message and is not validated against a whitelist. The event `ASDSent` is emitted before the transfer and no state reconciliation occurs. Combined with the fact that `_depositNoteToASDVault` mints ASD at that same unvalidated address, an attacker controls the "ASD token" contract entirely.
hypotheses.impact: An attacker can supply a fake ASD contract that returns `true` on `transfer` without moving tokens, so `lzCompose` completes successfully while the sender's funds remain in the fake contract; the sender/receiver gets nothing and the attacker keeps the NOTE/asdUSDC-equivalent value.
hypotheses.recommendation: Maintain an on-chain whitelist of valid canto ASD vault addresses and require `_cantoAsdAddress` to be whitelisted before any deposit/transfer.

hypotheses.title: ASDRouter _refundToken ignores failed transfer return value
hypotheses.description: `IERC20(_tokenAddress).transfer(_refundAddress, _amount)` does not check the return value. Some ERC20 tokens (e.g., USDT-like) return `false` instead of reverting on failure. If the transfer fails silently, the function continues, emits a `TokenRefund` event, and the tokens remain stuck in the router while the user believes they were refunded. Since `lzCompose` must not revert, this silent failure is especially dangerous.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker uses a whitelisted USDC version that returns `false` on transfer failure (or a token with transfer fees/blacklist). 2. `_refundToken` is called, transfer returns `false`, but no revert occurs. 3. Tokens remain in the router; attacker or anyone can later sweep them if a recovery path exists, or they are permanently stuck.
hypotheses.impact: User funds permanently stuck in the router; false refund event misleads off-chain monitoring.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransfer` in `_refundToken` and handle the failure case (e.g., emit a distinct event and retain tokens for manual recovery).

hypotheses.title: Incorrect decimal handling in ASDUSDC deposit/withdraw
hypotheses.description: The `deposit` function calculates `amountToMint = _amount * (10 ** (this.decimals() - ERC20(_usdcVersion).decimals()))`. If the USDC version has more decimals than ASDUSDC (18), the subtraction underflows, causing a revert. Conversely, if the USDC version has fewer decimals, the multiplication may overflow or produce incorrect amounts. The `withdraw` function has the same issue with division. This can lead to incorrect minting/burning of asdUSDC and loss of funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deposits a USDC version with decimals > 18 (if whitelisted). 2. The subtraction underflows, reverting the transaction. 3. Alternatively, if a USDC version with decimals < 18 is used, the attacker can deposit a small amount and receive a disproportionately large amount of asdUSDC due to incorrect scaling.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect accounting of asdUSDC balances, leading to loss of funds for the protocol or users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Normalize decimals using a safe scaling factor, e.g., `amountToMint = _amount * 10**18 / 10**ERC20(_usdcVersion).decimals()`, and ensure the result is correctly scaled.

hypotheses.title: _sendASD forwards msg.value to attacker-controlled OFT address
hypotheses.description: `_sendASD` performs `payable(_payload._cantoAsdAddress).call{value: _payload._feeForSend}(...)` where `_cantoAsdAddress` comes from the attacker-controlled composed message. There is no whitelist check that `_cantoAsdAddress` is a legitimate ASDOFT contract. An attacker can set `_cantoAsdAddress` to an arbitrary contract that accepts ETH, causing the router to forward its native balance to the attacker's contract while the router believes it is paying a LayerZero fee.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends a composed message with `_cantoAsdAddress = attackerContract` and `_dstLzEid != cantoLzEID`. 2) Router reaches `_sendASD`, checks `msg.value >= _feeForSend`, then calls `attackerContract` with `_feeForSend` ETH. 3) Attacker's contract receives the ETH; the router's `_refundToken` path is never reached because the call "succeeds".
hypotheses.impact: Theft of native ETH from the router; ASD tokens remain stuck or mis-accounted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Whitelist valid ASDOFT addresses (or derive them from a trusted registry) before making value-bearing calls; never forward `msg.value` to an address supplied in the message payload.

hypotheses.title: ASDUSDC deposit/withdraw decimal scaling can truncate to zero
hypotheses.description: `amountToWithdraw = _amount / (10 ** (this.decimals() - ERC20(_usdcVersion).decimals()))`. If `_amount` is smaller than the scaling factor (e.g., user withdraws a tiny asdUSDC amount when USDC has fewer decimals), the division truncates to zero. The user's asdUSDC is burned but they receive zero USDC. Conversely, `deposit` multiplies, which is safe, but the asymmetry means small withdrawals lose funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (or any user) calls `withdraw` with `_amount` less than `10 ** (18 - usdcDecimals)`. 2. `_burn` destroys the asdUSDC. 3. `amountToWithdraw` is 0, so no USDC is transferred. 4. User loses their asdUSDC for nothing.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds via truncation; asdUSDC burned without corresponding USDC payout.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_amount` to be a multiple of the scaling factor, or compute `amountToWithdraw` first and require it to be > 0 before burning.

hypotheses.title: lzCompose refund path reverts and traps tokens when token transfer fails
hypotheses.description: `_refundToken` is the designated safety net when lzCompose processing fails, and the doc comment states lzCompose "Cannot revert anywhere." However `_refundToken` uses `IERC20(_tokenAddress).transfer(...)` without a try/catch or return-value check, and unconditionally calls `payable(_refundAddress).transfer(_nativeAmount)`. If the destination token's transfer reverts (e.g. a paused/blacklisted recipient, or a token that reverts on zero transfer) or the native transfer reverts, the whole lzCompose call reverts, defeating the refund and leaving the OFT/USDC/NOTE permanently stuck in the router.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user whose cantoRefundAddress is a contract that reverts on receiving native tokens, or a receiver address that rejects the token) bridges an OFT with a composed message. 2) The swap or deposit fails (or attacker sets a bad minAmountASD), so the code path reaches `_refundToken`. 3) `IERC20.transfer` or `payable(_refundAddress).transfer` reverts. 4) The entire lzCompose execution reverts; LZ executor cannot deliver; tokens held by ASDRouter have no alternative sweep/recovery function.
hypotheses.impact: Bridged tokens become permanently locked in ASDRouter with no recovery path (no rescue/sweep function exists), and the LZ compose message cannot be replayed to a fixed refund address.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap the token transfer in a low-level `call` and ignore failure, or use a pull-based refund mechanism (credit a mapping). Also use `call{value:...}` for native refunds instead of `transfer`. Add an owner-callable rescue for stranded tokens.

hypotheses.title: lzCompose trusts composeFrom as refund address without verifying sender
hypotheses.description: When the composed message length is invalid, the router refunds the OFT tokens to `OFTComposeMsgCodec.bytes32ToAddress(composeFrom)` — an attacker-controlled field inside the message payload. The function never verifies that `_from`/`_guid` correspond to a legitimate LayerZero-delivered message, nor that `composeFrom` matches the actual sender on the source chain. Any address that can invoke `lzCompose` (or a malicious peer OFT) can craft a message with an arbitrary `composeFrom` and cause the router to transfer its held OFT balance to the attacker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys/controls an OFT-compatible contract on a source chain (or uses any whitelisted USDC OFT) and sends a composed message to the router with `composeMsg.length != 224`. 2) The router's `lzCompose` is invoked by the LZ executor with the attacker's `composeFrom` embedded. 3) Router calls `_refundToken` transferring `amountLD` of `_from` tokens to the attacker's address. 4) Attacker repeats to drain any OFT tokens the router holds.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of OFT tokens held by the router; loss of funds for legitimate users whose tokens are in-flight.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `_from` is a trusted/whitelisted OFT and that `composeFrom` corresponds to the actual source-chain sender (e.g., via `_srcEid` + peer mapping), or refund to a router-controlled address rather than an attacker-supplied one.

hypotheses.title: ASDRouter refunds wrong token address on swap failure
hypotheses.description: When `_swapOFTForNote` fails, the code calls `_refundToken(_guid, asdUSDC, payload._cantoRefundAddress, amountUSDC, ...)`. However, `amountUSDC` is the amount of asdUSDC minted by `ASDUSDC.deposit`, and the refund transfers asdUSDC (the wrapper) to the refund address. But the original OFT tokens were already deposited into ASDUSDC and are now held by ASDUSDC, not the router. The refund address receives asdUSDC instead of the original OFT, and the router's asdUSDC balance may be insufficient because the deposit minted asdUSDC to the router but the swap failure path assumes the router still holds it. More critically, the OFT tokens are now stuck in ASDUSDC with no way to recover them for the user.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker sends a composed message with a `_minAmountASD` that is guaranteed to fail the swap (e.g., extremely high min). 2. `lzCompose` deposits OFT into ASDUSDC, minting asdUSDC to the router. 3. Swap fails, `_refundToken` transfers asdUSDC (not the original OFT) to `_cantoRefundAddress`. 4. The original OFT is now permanently held by ASDUSDC with no withdrawal path for the user.
hypotheses.impact: User loses their original OFT tokens; they receive asdUSDC instead, which may not be redeemable for the specific OFT version they sent (or the router may not hold enough asdUSDC if multiple refunds occur).
hypotheses.recommendation: On swap failure, withdraw the OFT from ASDUSDC via `ASDUSDC.withdraw(_from, amountUSDC)` and refund the original OFT, or refund asdUSDC only after ensuring the router holds sufficient balance and documenting the behavior.

hypotheses.title: ASDRouter._swapOFTForNote casts uint to uint128 without bounds check
hypotheses.description: `uint128 amountConverted = uint128(_amount);` silently truncates if `_amount > type(uint128).max`. The OFT amount comes from the LZ compose message (`amountLD`), which is attacker-controlled via the source-chain send. A malicious sender can craft an amount that truncates to a small value, causing the router to swap only the truncated amount while the full `amountLD` was already deposited into asdUSDC. The excess asdUSDC remains in the router, and the user receives ASD for only the truncated amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends an OFT compose with `amountLD = 2^128 + X` (or any value > 2^128). 2) Router deposits full `amountLD` into asdUSDC, receiving full asdUSDC. 3) `_swapOFTForNote` truncates to `X`, swaps only `X` worth, and returns `X`-based NOTE. 4) Attacker receives ASD for `X`; the remaining `2^128` worth of asdUSDC is stranded in the router (or refunded incorrectly). 5) Attacker can repeat to drain value or lock funds.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds (excess asdUSDC stranded in router), incorrect ASD minted, potential value extraction if router balance is later swept.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_amount <= type(uint128).max` before casting, or use a safe cast that reverts.

hypotheses.title: Spot price manipulation via Ambient swap without TWAP or oracle
hypotheses.description: The swap relies on `ICrocImpact.calcImpact` to estimate output and enforce `_minAmountNote`, but this is a spot-price calculation on the Ambient pool. An attacker can manipulate the pool price via a flash loan or large swap immediately before the `lzCompose` call, causing `calcImpact` to return a favorable (or unfavorable) result. Since `_minAmountNote` is user-supplied and the swap uses `crocSwapAddress.call`, the actual swap may execute at a manipulated price, and the `calcImpact` check can be bypassed if the attacker controls the pool state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker flash-loans a large amount of USDC or NOTE. 2. Manipulates the Ambient pool price to make `calcImpact` return a value >= `_minAmountNote` while the actual swap returns less. 3. Calls `lzCompose` with a crafted message. 4. The swap executes at the manipulated price, and the attacker profits from the price difference or drains value from the pool.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds from the pool or from the user's swapped amount due to price manipulation; the `_minAmountNote` check is ineffective against spot-price manipulation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a TWAP oracle or Chainlink price feed to validate the swap price, or enforce a stricter slippage check based on the actual swap output rather than `calcImpact`.

hypotheses.title: Missing minimum-out enforcement in Ambient swap
hypotheses.description: The `crocSwapAddress.call` passes `uintMinAmount` as the minimum output, but the `calcImpact` check is done before the swap and can be manipulated. The actual swap may return less than `_minAmountNote` if the pool state changes between the `calcImpact` call and the swap. Since the swap is executed via a low-level call, the return value is decoded but not checked against `_minAmountNote` after the swap. This allows the swap to succeed with less output than the user specified.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a pending `lzCompose` transaction. 2. Front-runs it with a large swap that moves the pool price. 3. The `calcImpact` check passes based on the old state, but the actual swap returns less than `_minAmountNote`. 4. The user receives less NOTE than expected, and the attacker profits from the price movement.
hypotheses.impact: User receives less NOTE than specified, leading to loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: After the swap, verify that the actual output (`amountNote`) is >= `_minAmountNote` before proceeding; revert or refund if not.

hypotheses.title: lzCompose performs external calls before state reconciliation, enabling reentrancy
hypotheses.description: In `lzCompose`, the contract approves `asdUSDC`, calls `deposit`, swaps via `crocSwapAddress`, and calls `_depositNoteToASDVault` — all external calls — while relying on `msg.value` and prior state (e.g. token balances) for subsequent refund/send decisions. Any of these external calls (particularly `ASDOFT.mint` on a malicious or compromised vault, or the swap call into an attacker-influenced pool) can reenter `lzCompose` or `_refundToken`. Because the contract holds transient token balances between steps, a reentrant invocation could exploit the intermediate balances or double-refund.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user-supplied `_cantoAsdAddress` (an attacker-deployed contract exposing `mint(uint256)`) is passed in the compose payload. When `_depositNoteToASDVault` calls `mint`, the attacker's contract reenters `lzCompose` with a crafted `_message` and drains/refunds the still-held `$NOTE` or `asdUSDC` balances that belong to the outer call.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of funds held in the router during an in-flight compose (asdUSDC, NOTE, ASD), or inconsistent refunds causing loss to the original sender.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `lzCompose`, zero out intermediate balances or use pull-payment pattern, and validate `_cantoAsdAddress` against a whitelist.

hypotheses.title: asdUSDC deposit mints extra tokens via decimals mismatch trick
hypotheses.description: The minted amount is computed as `_amount * 10**(this.decimals() - ERC20(_usdcVersion).decimals())`. If a whitelisted USDC version has more decimals than asdUSDC (18), the exponent is negative and the multiplication underflows/reverts—but if the version has fewer decimals (e.g. 6), the multiplier is 1e12, minting 1e12 asdUSDC per USDC unit. Since the same multiplier is applied to all versions regardless of their own decimals, a depositor of a version with fewer decimals than 18 receives massively more asdUSDC than the value deposited, and can then withdraw from a different, higher-decimal version's balance (if the arithmetic happens to allow) or otherwise dilute. More importantly, `withdraw` performs integer division without accounting for the same scaling on the way out, so balances diverge.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner whitelists two USDC versions with different decimals (e.g. 6-decimal USDC and 18-decimal USDC). 2) Attacker deposits into the 6-decimal version receiving 1e12 asdUSDC per unit. 3) Attacker calls `withdraw` against an 18-decimal version, draining `usdcBalances[18dec]` which was contributed by other users. 4) Repeat until pools are drained.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of other depositors' USDC; `usdcBalances` per-version accounting becomes meaningless and the wrapper becomes insolvent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Normalize balances internally (track deposits in 18-decimal space) or store per-version share accounting and require decimals==18 for asdUSDC or explicit conversion both on deposit and withdrawal.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can freeze router refunds via cantoRefundAddress native-token revert
hypotheses.description: `_refundToken` forwards `_nativeAmount` (up to `msg.value`) to `_refundAddress` using `payable(...).transfer`, which forwards a fixed 2300 gas stipend. If `_refundAddress` is a smart contract with a fallback that consumes more than 2300 gas or simply reverts, this call always reverts, and since the requirement is "must not revert," the whole lzCompose reverts, blocking delivery of the message and leaving the bridged amount stuck in the router. The refund address is fully attacker-controlled via the compose payload, so an attacker can grief by choosing such an address, or any user can accidentally lock their own message.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts an OftComposeMessage with `_cantoRefundAddress` pointing to a contract whose receive/fallback reverts. 2) Attacker initiates a bridge with an amount/min that will force the refund branch (e.g. unwhitelisted OFT or invalid minAmountASD). 3) lzCompose reaches `_refundToken`. 4) `payable(_refundAddress).transfer(_nativeAmount)` reverts, causing the whole lzCompose to revert and the bridged tokens to remain locked.
hypotheses.impact: Funds and compose message delivery become permanently blocked; the router accumulates stranded token balances with no recovery.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `transfer` with a `call{value:...}` that does not revert on failure, and/or decouple native refund from token refund so the token transfer still completes.

hypotheses.title: ASDRouter enables double minting of ASD by replaying lzCompose on same USDC tokens
hypotheses.description: `lzCompose` is externally callable (IOAppComposer interface) and the router does not verify that `_guid` is unique or that it was actually dispatched by the LZ endpoint (no `msg.sender == endpoint` check). It decodes `amountLD` from the caller-supplied `_message`, then calls `ASDUSDC.deposit(_from, amountLD)` which does `transferFrom(msg.sender=router, this, amountLD)`. Since tokens already sitting on the router (e.g. refunds, dust, prior failed sends) are approved and used, an attacker can craft a fake `_message` with a valid `_from` whitelisted USDC version and arbitrary amountLD up to the router's balance, causing the router to convert its own held tokens into ASD deposited to any `_cantoAsdAddress` and push ASD to any receiver. The attacker can repeat with fresh guids since there's no replay protection.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes router holds some USDC or funnels a tiny amount into the router's balance. 2) Attacker calls `lzCompose(from=USDC, guid=arbitrary, _message=crafted with amountLD matching held balance, composeFrom=self, payload targeting own `_cantoAsdAddress`). 3) Router approves and deposits the held USDC into ASDUSDC, swaps, mints ASD, and forwards to attack-controlled destination. 4) Repeat.
hypotheses.impact: Router-held USDC (including refund-bound tokens) can be stolen/minted into attacker-chosen ASD destination; drain of refundable balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Gate `lzCompose` to the LZ endpoint (`require msg.sender == address(endpoint)`) and verify `_from`/srcEid against the actual endpoint message; track used guids for replay protection.

hypotheses.title: ASDOFT mint/burn assumes 1:1 NOTE:asD but cNote exchange rate drifts
hypotheses.description: `mint` transfers `_amount` NOTE, mints `_amount` cNOTE, and mints `_amount` asD. `burn` redeems `_amount` underlying and burns `_amount` asD. This assumes cNOTE's exchange rate is exactly 1:1 with NOTE. In Compound-style cTokens, the exchange rate increases over time as interest accrues. `redeemUnderlying(_amount)` will succeed as long as the contract holds enough underlying, but the contract's cNOTE balance decreases by `_amount / exchangeRate` cNOTE, not `_amount`. Over time, the contract accumulates surplus cNOTE (from interest), which is intended for `withdrawCarry`. However, if the exchange rate ever drops below 1 (e.g., bad debt), `burn` will fail or the contract becomes insolvent, and `withdrawCarry`'s `maximumWithdrawable` calculation can underflow.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. If cNOTE exchange rate drops below 1 (e.g., due to a Compound bad debt event), `balanceOfUnderlying(address(this)) < totalSupply()`. 2. `withdrawCarry` computes `maximumWithdrawable = balanceOfUnderlying - totalSupply()`, which underflows and reverts. 3. `burn` may also fail if the contract cannot redeem enough underlying. 4. Users cannot burn asD for NOTE.
hypotheses.impact: asD becomes unredeemable; users lose funds; `withdrawCarry` permanently reverts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `exchangeRateStored` to compute the correct cNOTE amounts, and guard `withdrawCarry` against underflow by checking `balanceOfUnderlying >= totalSupply()`.

hypotheses.title: recover() mints asdUSDC to owner for pre-existing balances, diluting holders
hypotheses.description: `recover` computes `balanceOf(this) - usdcBalances[version]` and mints the corresponding asdUSDC to the owner. Any mismatch between `usdcBalances` and actual balance (e.g. due to donations, airdrops, or direct transfers of the same USDC version—which are untrusted-actor reachable) can be harvested by the owner at any time, capturing value that economically belongs to existing asdUSDC holders via dilution of shares. Because `recover` increments `usdcBalances` and mints, no `msg.sender` controls it beyond owner, but the trigger (a donation from an attacker or coincidental balance) can be set up by any external actor to convert this into a systematic owner-extraction path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Any user transfers a small amount of a whitelisted USDC version directly to the contract. 2) Owner calls `recover(version)` repeatedly and mints himself asdUSDC for the difference. 3) Owner redeems against other versions' backing.
hypotheses.impact: Holders' per-token backing decreases; effective theft of underlying deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Disallow `recover` from minting when it dilutes existing holders, or require the recovered amount to be held in reserve without new mint, or event-log and route to a treasury with holder consent.

hypotheses.title: ASDRouter._sendASD uses minAmountLD = amountLD with no slippage tolerance
hypotheses.description: In the cross-chain branch, `SendParam` sets `minAmountLD: _amount` equal to `amountLD: _amount`. LayerZero OFT applies a `sharedDecimals` conversion and may deduct dust during `_removeDust`, so the received amount on the destination can be less than `_amount`. With `minAmountLD == amountLD`, the send will revert if any dust is removed, causing the entire compose to fail and the ASD to be refunded. This is a functional DoS for tokens whose local decimals exceed shared decimals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker triggers a cross-chain send where `_amount` is not a multiple of `10^(localDecimals - sharedDecimals)`. 2) OFT `_removeDust` reduces the amount, making `amountSentLD < minAmountLD`. 3) The send reverts, and the router refunds ASD to `_cantoRefundAddress`. 4) Attacker can grief legitimate users by forcing refunds, or the user's intended transfer never completes.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain transfers fail for non-dust-multiple amounts; users receive refunds instead of destination tokens, breaking the intended flow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `minAmountLD` to `_amount - dust` or apply the same `_removeDust` logic before constructing `SendParam`.

hypotheses.title: Missing slippage protection in ASD send via LayerZero
hypotheses.description: When sending ASD tokens cross-chain, the code sets `minAmountLD: _amount` in the SendParam, which is correct for a 1:1 OFT. However, the `_feeForSend` is taken from the user-supplied payload and passed directly as `nativeFee` without verifying it matches the actual LayerZero fee. If the actual fee is higher, the send reverts and tokens are refunded; if lower, excess is lost. More critically, the user controls `_feeForSend` and the contract forwards `msg.value` from the compose call, so a user could underpay or the send could fail silently.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker crafts a compose message with `_feeForSend` set to 0 or a very low value. 2. The `IOFT.send` call is made with insufficient native fee. 3. The call reverts, and `_refundToken` is invoked, refunding ASD tokens to `_cantoRefundAddress` (attacker-controlled). 4. Attacker receives ASD tokens on Canto without completing the intended cross-chain transfer, potentially bypassing intended flow.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can force refunds to an arbitrary address, potentially griefing or extracting value if the refund address differs from the intended receiver.
hypotheses.recommendation: Query the actual LayerZero fee via `IOFT.quoteSend` and require `msg.value >= quotedFee`, or restrict `_feeForSend` to be validated against the quoted fee.

hypotheses.title: No check for stale or zero price from calcImpact
hypotheses.description: The `calcImpact` call returns `baseFlow` and `quoteFlow`, which are used to check against `_minAmountNote`. However, there is no check for whether these values are zero or stale. If the pool is empty or the oracle is stale, `calcImpact` could return zero flows, and the check `-baseFlow < minAmountInt` would pass if `minAmountInt` is also zero, allowing a swap with no output. Additionally, if `calcImpact` reverts or returns unexpected values, the swap could proceed with incorrect assumptions.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker waits for the pool to be in a state where `calcImpact` returns zero or stale values (e.g., low liquidity). 2. Calls `lzCompose` with `_minAmountNote` set to 0. 3. The check passes, and the swap executes, potentially returning zero NOTE. 4. Attacker receives ASD tokens minted from zero NOTE, or the swap fails and tokens are refunded.
hypotheses.impact: User receives less than expected or zero NOTE, leading to loss of funds or incorrect minting of ASD tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add checks for `baseFlow != 0` and `quoteFlow != 0`, and ensure `_minAmountNote > 0` to prevent zero-output swaps.

hypotheses.title: Refund address can be arbitrary, enabling token theft
hypotheses.description: The `_refundToken` function transfers tokens to `_refundAddress`, which is taken from the user-supplied `payload._cantoRefundAddress`. There is no validation that this address is the original sender or a trusted party. An attacker can craft a compose message with `_cantoRefundAddress` set to their own address, causing any failed swap or deposit to refund tokens to the attacker instead of the legitimate user.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker sends a cross-chain message with a crafted payload where `_cantoRefundAddress` is the attacker's address. 2. The swap or deposit fails (e.g., due to insufficient liquidity or invalid vault). 3. `_refundToken` transfers the tokens to the attacker's address. 4. Attacker receives the tokens without completing the intended transfer.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of tokens from the legitimate user or the protocol.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `_cantoRefundAddress` matches the original sender (`composeFrom`) or restrict refunds to the original sender.

hypotheses.title: ASDOFT.withdrawCarry reads maximumWithdrawable before redeem, no reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: `maximumWithdrawable = balanceOfUnderlying - totalSupply()` is computed, then `redeemUnderlying` is executed followed by a NOTE transfer. There is no `nonReentrant` guard, and `mint`/`burn` in the same contract can be invoked during the redeem callback (or from a malicious cNote implementation). Because the check is performed before the effect, a reentrant `burn` (which reduces totalSupply) during `redeemUnderlying` causes a subsequent outer transfer to send more than `maximumWithdrawable` (computed pre-reentrancy) permits relative to the new supply.
hypotheses.impact: The 1:1 peg between NOTE and asD can be broken; late burners find insufficient NOTE backing, causing loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `withdrawCarry`, `mint`, `burn`; recompute `maximumWithdrawable` after all state updates, or snapshot and enforce supply invariant at end.

hypotheses.title: _refundToken allows arbitrary native send and token transfer to user-chosen address
hypotheses.description: `_refundToken` sends both ERC20 tokens and native `msg.value` to `_refundAddress`, which is user-controlled (`payload._cantoRefundAddress` or `composeFrom`). The transfer happens before any reentrancy guard and can trigger a receiving contract's fallback, which may reenter `lzCompose`. Additionally, when `_tokenAddress` equals `_cantoAsdAddress` (attacker-supplied), the transfer can be an arbitrary token — this lets the attacker cause the router to transfer any held balance by pointing the "ASD token" at an arbitrary ERC20.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker crafts a compose message whose composed payload leads to `_refundToken(_guid, someWhitelistedUSDC, attacker, amount, msg.value, ...)`, then in the refund target's fallback reenters `lzCompose` to trigger another refund against still-present balances.
hypotheses.impact: Double-refund / drain of held USDC or NOTE from the router.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `_refundAddress` is not a contract or use pull-payments; transfer native via `call` and add a reentrancy guard on `lzCompose`.

hypotheses.title: _swapOFTForNote hardcodes 128-bit cast, DoS for large amounts
hypotheses.description: `uint128 amountConverted = uint128(_amount)` silently truncates if `_amount` exceeds type(uint128).max. There is no check that `_amount <= type(uint128).max`. For large bridged amounts, the swap executes on a truncated amount, causing incorrect swap accounting and potential asset loss, or reverts downstream.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user bridges an amount above 2^128 of the OFT; the router swaps only the truncated 128-bit value but the router's balance reflects the full amount, leaving the residual stranded.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong swap amount, stuck residual funds in router; effectively a DoS/loss for large transfers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(_amount <= type(uint128).max)` before casting, or refund the message when out of range.

hypotheses.title: ASDRouter leaves open approval to ASDUSDC and ASD vaults
hypotheses.description: `IERC20(_from).approve(asdUSDC, amountLD)` and `IERC20(noteAddress).approve(_asdVault, _amountNote)` are set without resetting to zero after use. If the deposit or mint consumes less than the approved amount (e.g., due to rounding or partial consumption), residual allowance remains. An untrusted actor who later gains control of the spender (or if the spender is upgradeable/malicious) can drain the router's token balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker triggers a compose where the ASD vault mint consumes less than `_amountNote` (or the deposit path leaves residual allowance). 2. Residual allowance to `_asdVault` or `asdUSDC` remains. 3. If the spender contract is compromised or upgradeable, attacker calls `transferFrom(router, attacker, residual)` to drain tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of any tokens held by the router (OFT, NOTE, asdUSDC) via residual allowances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reset approvals to zero after each use, or use `SafeERC20.forceApprove` with exact amounts and clear afterward.

hypotheses.title: ASDOFT.burn redeems cNOTE without burning caller's ASD first
hypotheses.description: `burn` calls `cNoteToken.redeemUnderlying(_amount)` (redeeming NOTE from the shared cNOTE pool) before `_burn(msg.sender, _amount)`. If the caller has insufficient ASD balance, `_burn` reverts, but the redeem already happened in the same tx so it reverts too — however the ordering means any reentrancy or token with hooks could observe state inconsistently. More importantly, `mint`/`burn` are permissionless and rely on 1:1 accounting; `withdrawCarry` is `onlyOwner` but the invariant `balanceOfUnderlying >= totalSupply` can be violated if `redeemUnderlying` returns less than `_amount` due to cNOTE liquidity, letting a burner extract more NOTE than ASD burned relative to pool.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker mints ASD with NOTE. 2) When cNOTE has accrued interest, attacker burns ASD to redeem NOTE; if `redeemUnderlying` succeeds but returns less NOTE than `_amount` (cToken shortfall), the ASD is burned for less value, or conversely the attacker can time burns to extract interest that should back other holders. 3) Repeated mint/burn around interest accrual skews the 1:1 backing.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency of the ASD:NOTE peg; later burners cannot redeem 1:1.
hypotheses.recommendation: Burn ASD before redeeming, and verify the actual NOTE received equals `_amount` (or adjust accounting) to preserve the 1:1 invariant.

hypotheses.title: ASDOFT.burn redeems NOTE before burning asD shares
hypotheses.description: `burn` calls `cNoteToken.redeemUnderlying(_amount)` (which transfers NOTE to this contract prior to `_burn(msg.sender, _amount)`) and then `SafeERC20.safeTransfer(note, msg.sender, _amount)`. Through the Compound-cNote `redeemUnderlying` callback path (or via a token with hooks if NOTE were replaceable), an attacker can reenter `burn` while `totalSupply()` has not yet been decremented, effectively burning against stale supply and redeeming against a contract that still holds the NOTE. Even without reentrancy in cNote, the ordering (redeem → burn → transfer) means an intervening reentrant `mint`/`burn` sees an incorrect totalSupply.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `burn`; during `redeemUnderlying`, reenter `withdrawCarry` or `burn`/`mint` to manipulate `balanceOfUnderlying` vs `totalSupply`, then rely on the outer call's post-state to extract more NOTE than burned.
hypotheses.impact: Accounting desync between cNOTE balance and ASD supply; attacker can redeem more underlying per asD than intended, draining carry and breaking 1:1 peg.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reorder to `_burn` first, then redeem and transfer, and/or add a nonReentrant modifier to `mint`/`burn`/`withdrawCarry`.

hypotheses.title: _sendASD transfer return value ignored, tokens can be silently stuck
hypotheses.description: When `_payload._dstLzEid == cantoLzEID`, the function performs `ASDOFT(...).transfer(_payload._dstReceiver, _amount)` but ignores the boolean return value. Some ERC20/OFT implementations (or upgradeable ones) can return false instead of reverting; the router would still emit ASDSent and consider the operation successful, leaving the minted ASD tokens in the router with no further action. Also, if ASD transfer reverts (paused/blocked receiver), the whole lzCompose reverts and the underlying already-swapped NOTE is stuck in the router with no recovery.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker supplies `_dstReceiver` as an address that causes ASDOFT.transfer to return false (e.g. a token with return-false semantics) or revert (e.g. blacklisted by an upgradable ASD implementation). 2) lzCompose proceeds to `_sendASD` and calls transfer. 3) If revert: entire txn reverts, tokens already minted into the router remain stuck. If false return: ASDSent is emitted, accounting is wrong, tokens remain in router.
hypotheses.impact: ASD tokens minted by the router become stranded with no recovery path; the recipient never receives their bridged value.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransfer` and/or check the return value; add a recovery/sweep function for tokens held by the router.

hypotheses.title: _swapOFTForNote uses attacker-controlled token address in swap
hypotheses.description: `_swapOFTForNote` is called with `asdUSDC` (the router's own token) as `_oftAddress`, but the swap target `crocSwapAddress` and pool parameters are fixed. However, the function trusts `_minAmountNote` from the attacker payload and the `crocSwapAddress.call` return data is decoded without verifying the swap actually occurred. If the pool doesn't exist or the call returns malformed data, the router may still proceed with `successfulSwap = true` and a bogus `amountNote`, leading to incorrect ASD minting or refunds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sets `_minAmountASD = 0` and crafts a message that causes `crocSwapAddress.call` to return data that decodes to a large `amountNote`. 2) Router proceeds to `_depositNoteToASDVault` with an inflated amount, potentially minting ASD against no real NOTE, or triggering a refund of the wrong amount.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect accounting; potential minting of unbacked ASD or loss of funds via refunds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the swap result against actual token balance deltas (measure NOTE balance before/after) rather than trusting decoded return data; enforce a non-zero minimum.

hypotheses.title: asdOFT.withdrawCarry reads stale balance to size max withdrawal
hypotheses.description: `maximumWithdrawable = balanceOfUnderlying(this) - totalSupply()`. `balanceOfUnderlying` uses cToken's current exchange rate, which can fluctuate (interest is monotonic up, but slashing/liquidation of underlying via Compound is possible) and Note decimals must match asdOFT. If cNOTE accrues interest, this "carry" is withdrawable by the owner, but the check ignores pending exchange-rate changes between read and redeem: the actual redeemed `_amount` may be less than `maximumWithdrawable` after the cToken's exchangeRate shifts (or after another actor mints/burns), potentially leaving the contract under-collateralized relative to outstanding asdOFT supply. Since `mint` and `burn` are permissionless and change `totalSupply`, an attacker can front-run owner's `withdrawCarry` by minting, then burning right after, to leave the invariant broken.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes owner's withdrawCarry tx. 2) Attacker mints large asdOFT (locks 1:1 Note). 3) After owner withdraws carry sized off a totalSupply that included attacker's mint, attacker burns immediately, redeeming Note from cNOTE. Net effect: asdOFT outstanding backed by less than 1:1 because the carry was sized assuming the temporary inflation.
hypotheses.impact: asdOFT becomes undercollateralized; remaining holders cannot burn 1:1, loss of peg.
hypotheses.recommendation: Size carry using a stable accounting variable (e.g. tracked principal deposits) rather than current totalSupply, or disallow onlyOwner withdrawal when the final remaining backing ratio after withdrawal would be < 1.0. Consider locking mint/burn around carry withdrawal.

hypotheses.title: ASDRouter _sendASD uses msg.value for fee but refunds full msg.value
hypotheses.description: In the cross-chain branch, `_sendASD` calls the OFT with `{value: _payload._feeForSend}` but the outer `lzCompose` received `msg.value` which may be larger. If the send succeeds, the remaining `msg.value - _feeForSend` is never refunded to anyone and remains stuck in the router. If the send fails, `_refundToken` is called with `msg.value` (the full amount), which may exceed the actual remaining balance if the OFT call already consumed `_feeForSend` before reverting (though a revert would return the value). The accounting is inconsistent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker sends a compose with `_feeForSend` less than `msg.value`. 2. `_sendASD` succeeds, consuming only `_feeForSend`. 3. Excess `msg.value - _feeForSend` remains in the router. 4. Attacker (or anyone) cannot recover it, but it accumulates; if a future refund path uses `msg.value` incorrectly, funds can be misdirected.
hypotheses.impact: Native tokens stuck in the router; potential over-refund if `msg.value` is used as the refund amount after partial consumption.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the actual native fee consumed and refund the remainder to `_cantoRefundAddress` explicitly.

hypotheses.title: ASDUSDC.recover mints to owner from unaccounted balance, manipulable via donation
hypotheses.description: `recover` computes `balanceOf(this) - usdcBalances[_usdcVersion]` and mints asdUSDC to the owner. While `onlyOwner`, the amount is derived from raw balance, so any external actor can donate USDC to inflate the recoverable amount; more critically, `deposit`/`withdraw` use `usdcBalances` per version but `withdraw` divides by `10**(decimals diff)` with integer truncation, allowing repeated small withdrawals to extract dust while burning less than proportional asdUSDC, and `recover` can be used to socialize that loss.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a tiny amount of a high-decimals whitelisted USDC version. 2) Attacker repeatedly calls `withdraw` with amounts that truncate to 0 USDC but still burn asdUSDC (or vice versa) to skew `usdcBalances`. 3) Over time `usdcBalances` diverges from actual balance; owner `recover` mints unbacked asdUSDC.
hypotheses.impact: Accounting drift between `usdcBalances` and real balances; unbacked asdUSDC minted, diluting holders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round withdrawals in favor of the protocol (require exact divisibility or round up burn), and base `recover` on tracked balances only.

hypotheses.title: ASDOFT.withdrawCarry can be front-run by burn to reduce maximumWithdrawable
hypotheses.description: `maximumWithdrawable = balanceOfUnderlying(this) - totalSupply()`. If `balanceOfUnderlying` grows slower than expected (e.g., due to cNOTE exchange rate rounding or a redeem that returns slightly less), the subtraction can underflow and revert. More subtly, a user can burn asD to reduce `totalSupply`, which increases `maximumWithdrawable` — but the owner is trusted, so this is not an attack. However, if `balanceOfUnderlying` ever falls below `totalSupply` (e.g., due to cNOTE loss), `withdrawCarry` reverts and carry cannot be withdrawn, and `burn` may also fail to redeem 1:1.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by untrusted actor; relies on cNOTE exchange rate behavior. If cNOTE's `balanceOfUnderlying` returns a value less than `totalSupply` due to rounding, `withdrawCarry` reverts, and the 1:1 invariant for `burn` is broken (users cannot redeem full NOTE).
hypotheses.impact: Carry withdrawal DoS; potential insolvency of the 1:1 NOTE:asD peg if cNOTE underperforms.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a checked subtraction with a clear error, and consider a buffer or fallback when `balanceOfUnderlying < totalSupply`.

hypotheses.title: Owner can freeze ASDRouter by de-whitelisting source OFT mid-flight
hypotheses.description: lzCompose checks `ASDUSDC(asdUSDC).whitelistedUSDCVersions(_from)` and refunds to `payload._cantoRefundAddress` if false. Combined with `_refundToken`'s use of `IERC20.transfer` and (for the whitelist branch) routing to a user-supplied refund address, a mismatch between the whitelist and a receiver address that rejects tokens causes a permanent revert. While the whitelist is owner-controlled (out-of-lens), the refund path's revert behavior converts a config change into an unrecoverable stuck-funds state for in-flight messages.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly attacker-exploitable without owner action. However, an in-flight message with an invalid whitelist state routes to `_refundToken`; if `_cantoRefundAddress` cannot receive the token (e.g. blacklisted by USDC), the refund reverts and the compose message is permanently undeliverable, freezing the bridged USDC in the router.
hypotheses.impact: Bridged USDC/ASD becomes permanently stuck in ASDRouter for affected in-flight messages.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `_refundToken` non-reverting, or add a fallback that escrows tokens in the router with an owner/recipient pull mechanism.

hypotheses.title: lzCompose lacks replay protection on _guid
hypotheses.description: `lzCompose` does not track processed `_guid` values. While LayerZero's endpoint normally prevents duplicate delivery, the router itself has no internal nonce/guid guard, and the function is `external payable` with no access control. If the endpoint or a malicious peer ever re-delivers a message (or if the router is called directly in a test/misconfigured deployment), the same composed message can be re-executed, causing repeated swaps, deposits, or refunds against the router's balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a valid `_guid`/`_message` pair (e.g., from a prior legitimate delivery) and replays it if the endpoint allows re-delivery or if the router is invoked directly. 2) Router re-executes the swap/deposit/refund logic, draining balances or minting duplicate ASD.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate execution leading to loss of funds or incorrect accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Maintain a `mapping(bytes32 => bool) processed` keyed by `_guid` and revert on replay; also restrict `lzCompose` to the LZ endpoint.

hypotheses.title: asdUSDC.withdraw integer division truncates dust that stays in contract
hypotheses.description: `amountToWithdraw = _amount / 10**(this.decimals() - ERC20(_usdcVersion).decimals())` uses floor division. A user who withdrew at a non-multiple gets less USDC, and the residual asdUSDC-equivalent backing stays in the contract with no claim. The owner's `recover` path can later absorb this leftover as minted asdUSDC—again channeling holder value to the owner.
hypotheses.attackPath: Repeatedly withdraw fractional amounts to accumulate a small residual; owner calls `recover` to mint asdUSDC to itself for the leftover.
hypotheses.impact: Small but persistent value leakage from users to the owner.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round in the user's favour or track a per-account dust balance; or exclude recovered dust from `recover` minting.
